title: An Odia-American Civil Rights Lawyer Just Made History in Georgia — and the June Runoff Could Make More
excerpt: Rahul Garabadu's strong second-place finish in Gwinnett County's Senate primary puts an Indian American one election away from a seat no one from the community has ever held.
body:
The results from Georgia's May 19 primary elections are still being certified, but one outcome has already rewritten a small piece of South Asian American political history. Rahul Garabadu, a second-generation Odia-American civil rights attorney, captured 33.2 per cent of the vote in the Democratic primary for State Senate District 7, earning a spot in the June 16 runoff against State Representative Ruwa Romman, who led with 38.2 per cent. Educator Astrid Ross was eliminated with 28.6 per cent.

If Garabadu wins the runoff — and then the November general election in what is a solidly Democratic district — he would become the first person of Indian origin, and the first Odia American, ever to serve in the Georgia State Senate. The milestone would arrive in Gwinnett County, a suburban sprawl northeast of Atlanta that has transformed over two decades from a conservative white stronghold into one of the most ethnically diverse counties in the United States.

## A District Built by Immigration

Senate District 7 sits entirely within Gwinnett, covering Berkeley Lake, Duluth, and parts of Lawrenceville, Norcross, Peachtree Corners, and Suwanee. The county is now majority-minority, with a rapidly growing South Asian population anchored by Indian, Pakistani, and Bangladeshi families drawn by the area's technology jobs and relatively affordable housing. Georgia is home to more than 600,000 Asian American residents, and Gwinnett is where many of them have put down roots.

The seat opened after Democratic State Senator Nabilah Parkes — herself a historic figure as a Bangladeshi American in the legislature — resigned in March to run for lieutenant governor. Parkes, too, advanced to a runoff in her race on May 19, and could become the first South Asian and Asian American lieutenant governor nominee from any political party in Georgia history.

## The Candidate and His Platform

Garabadu, the son of Odia immigrants, built his career in civil rights law before entering politics. His legal work has included suing the state over electoral redistricting maps and challenging jail conditions — the kind of unglamorous, adversarial litigation that rarely attracts public attention but that shapes the infrastructure of democracy itself.

His campaign platform centres on three issues: the escalating cost of living in metro Atlanta, where housing prices have outpaced wage growth for a decade; robust protections for immigrant communities facing what he describes as an atmosphere of fear created by federal deportation policies; and expanding access to affordable healthcare. "Immigrants are fundamental to our economy — from our agricultural heartlands to our booming tech hubs," Garabadu said during the campaign. "They are our entrepreneurs, essential workers, and taxpayers who revitalize our communities."

## A Broader Wave

Garabadu's advance is part of what Indian American Impact, a political advocacy organisation, described as a series of "historic victories" across Georgia on May 19. Beyond Garabadu and Parkes, the group celebrated Jyot Singh winning the State House District 97 primary — positioning him to become the first Sikh elected official in Georgia history — along with Saira Draper securing the Senate District 44 primary and Akbar Ali locking down his renomination as Georgia's youngest state legislator in House District 106.

"Last night's results in Georgia speak to the growing political power and representation of our communities," said Chintan Patel, Indian American Impact's executive director. "We are thrilled to see so many South Asian leaders stepping into the halls of power."

## What the Diaspora Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora across the United States, the Georgia results are a signal worth reading carefully. The state's South Asian political class has grown from essentially zero representation a decade ago to a cohort now contesting — and winning — races at every level of state government. The shift mirrors demographic changes in other Sun Belt states with growing Indian populations, including Texas, North Carolina, and Virginia.

The June 16 runoff between Garabadu and Romman will test whether the Indian American community can consolidate support behind a candidate in a two-way race. Romman, a Palestinian American who currently represents House District 97, has her own historic profile and a larger vote share from the first round. But runoffs often reward ground-game intensity over name recognition, and Garabadu's civil rights network in Gwinnett runs deep.

For NRIs watching from afar, the race offers a concrete case study in a larger question: whether the diaspora's growing economic presence in American suburbs will translate into proportional political power, or whether representation will continue to lag behind population. Gwinnett County, where the answer is being written in real time, is a place worth watching.
